
# Week 10 – Sequelize SQL Comparison

## 1. GET /authors/:id/books

### SQL generated by Sequelize

```sql
SELECT
  "Author"."id",
  "Author"."name",
  "books"."id" AS "books.id",
  "books"."title" AS "books.title",
  "books"."genre" AS "books.genre",
  "books"."published_year" AS "books.published_year",
  "books"."author_id" AS "books.author_id"
FROM "authors" AS "Author"
LEFT OUTER JOIN "books" AS "books"
  ON "Author"."id" = "books"."author_id"
WHERE "Author"."id" = 1;
```

### SQL I would write manually

```sql
SELECT
  a.id,
  a.name,
  b.id,
  b.title,
  b.genre,
  b.published_year,
  b.author_id
FROM authors AS a
LEFT JOIN books AS b
  ON a.id = b.author_id
WHERE a.id = 1;
```

### Comparison

Sequelize generated a LEFT OUTER JOIN, which keeps the
author in the result even if they have no books.

Sequelize uses quoted table names and longer aliases,
such as "books.title". These aliases help Sequelize
organize the returned columns into related objects.

My SQL is shorter and easier to read, but both queries
retrieve the author and their associated books.




## 2. GET /members/:id/loans

### SQL generated by Sequelize

```sql
SELECT
  "Member"."id",
  "Member"."name",
  "Member"."email",
  "borrowedBooks"."id" AS "borrowedBooks.id",
  "borrowedBooks"."title" AS "borrowedBooks.title",
  "borrowedBooks"."genre" AS "borrowedBooks.genre",
  "borrowedBooks"."published_year" AS "borrowedBooks.published_year",
  "borrowedBooks"."author_id" AS "borrowedBooks.author_id",
  "borrowedBooks->Loan"."id" AS "borrowedBooks.Loan.id",
  "borrowedBooks->Loan"."loan_date" AS "borrowedBooks.Loan.loan_date",
  "borrowedBooks->Loan"."returned_at" AS "borrowedBooks.Loan.returned_at"
FROM "members" AS "Member"
LEFT OUTER JOIN (
  "loans" AS "borrowedBooks->Loan"
  INNER JOIN "books" AS "borrowedBooks"
    ON "borrowedBooks"."id" = "borrowedBooks->Loan"."book_id"
)
  ON "Member"."id" = "borrowedBooks->Loan"."member_id"
WHERE "Member"."id" = 1;
```

### SQL I would write manually

```sql
SELECT
  m.id AS member_id,
  m.name AS member_name,
  m.email,
  b.id AS book_id,
  b.title AS book_title,
  b.genre,
  b.published_year,
  b.author_id,
  l.id AS loan_id,
  l.loan_date,
  l.returned_at
FROM members m
LEFT JOIN (
  loans l
  INNER JOIN books b ON b.id = l.book_id
) ON m.id = l.member_id
WHERE m.id = 1;
```

### Comparison

Sequelize generated a query that joins three tables:
members, loans, and books.

It uses LEFT OUTER JOIN to keep the member in the result,
even if the member has not borrowed any books.

Inside that join, Sequelize uses INNER JOIN to connect
each loan to its book.

Sequelize also uses longer aliases such as
"borrowedBooks.Loan.loan_date" to organize the related
data into JavaScript objects.

My handwritten SQL uses shorter aliases like m, l,
and b, which makes it easier to read.

Both queries retrieve the member and their borrowing
information, including book titles and loan dates.
